en: Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
I bow to the Three-eyed One seated upon a corpse-throne, whose faces are turned toward him;

to Vārāhī, whose body is crimson; who has suddenly crushed the Lord of Serpents with her two primary arms, while holding with her other four left arms a skull-topped staff, a noose, Naraka, and the head of Brahmā.
Holding in his right hands a hand-dagger, a trident, an axe, and a *ḍamaru* drum— him who is named Heruka— I shall proclaim his sādhana, which has been concealed in the Mleccha language.
The *Cakrasaṃvara-guhyārtha-siddhimantra-samuccaya*. [In] Mleccha language [on purpose]:
Having summoned the Sugatas before me by means of the arrays of the seed-syllables within the moon in the heart, || 2 ||
Having worshipped with all forms of worship, one should recite the [mantra] beginning with the Three Jewels.

Having visualized everything as empty, the wise one should emerge with hosts of ḍākinīs from the syllable *hūṃ*— which consists of a universal lotus, sun, and vajra— and perform the ritual of driving in the stakes (*kīla*) and so forth.
In the element of space, the wise one should contemplate the dissolution of the four elements,
for by the assembly of all elements, he becomes the support of the universe.
This is its sequence:
One should fashion [the image] from cow-dung, blue lotus, or from the remaining dried veins and blood;
for the tortoise, it should be made of great conch-shell and be impenetrable.
It may have four arms and four faces, or likewise up to a hundred thousand arms.
The great wrathful deity with a white body is embraced by his consort holding a vajra and bell;
he is a hero adorned with a garland of skulls and his limbs are smeared with ashes;
his face is slightly terrifying with bared fangs, and he sits upon a great corpse.
His body, adorned with the six mudrās and crowned with a mass of matted hair, radiates a great cloud of victorious rays in all directions.
His right face is black, while his left is red and terrifying.
The primary face is great white, while the western one is blazing with gold;
it conquers even Kāla and Mṛtyu, and is joined with a khaṭvāṅga upon its limb.
A skull-cup and a vessel of wealth are applied as weapons to its mouths.
His wisdom is most formidable, with a girdle adorned by severed heads;
she holds a skull-bowl filled with entrails as her weapon, bearing his very color.
She dwells in mountain caves and thickets, or upon the shores of the great ocean.
And in that Ādisiddhi cremation ground, one should draw the maṇḍala.
The "enclosure" (saṃpuṭa) and the state of being enclosed is called the "vajra-chain.
One should pierce the lotus with the vajra, and then rotate it like a peacock's tail-feather.
One should attract [the deity] with the hook (aṅkuśa) and agitate with the mace (muṣala).
Then, according to the ritual procedure, one should expand the so-called vajra for the purpose of devouring.
Having joined it with the arrow of penetration, it becomes liquefied through the vidyā-mantra.
Just as the *dharmakāya* arises from the conjunction of the wood to be rubbed and the rubbing stick, so too did all the Buddhas, through their assembly, swiftly exhort me:
"Oṃ! O Vajrasattva of Great Bliss! Jaḥ Hūṃ Vaṃ Hoḥ! You are the one of supreme joy; behold! Thus they said.
As soon as you were thus exhorted, O bestower of happiness upon the world-system,
the Vajra-holder himself arose from me through his own mantra, according to the sequence of the ritual for manifestation,
from the two syllables Aṃ and Hūṃ in a liquid form.
Blue in color and most terrible, with a mandala blazing with red flames;
four-faced and most fearsome, adorned with twelve arms;
having completely overwhelmed the Lord of Umā, he sits upon the sun as his seat. || 18–19 ||
The primary face is deep black, the right is like a kunda flower,
the left is red and most terrifying, and the western face is radiant like gold.
He is endowed with his original weapons and is resplendent with three eyes.
Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, his face is grinning with wrath.
His consort is Vārāhī, red in color and most brilliantly radiant;
she is divine, possessing two arms and one face, and holds a vajra and a human skull-cup.
The empowerment from the four faces of the Blessed One:
Oṃ sumbha nisumbha huṃ hūṃ phaṭ;
oṃ gṛhṇa 2 huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja huṃ hūṃ phaṭ || [The Blessed One] from reverse order.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the dharmadhātu.
Thus is the service.
23. Oṃ ha. Vajrasattva is at the heart. Oṃ nama hi. Vairocana is at the head. Namaḥ.
Oṃ svāhā huḥ | Padmanarteśvara at the crown of the head. Oṃ vauṣaṭ he | Śrī Heruka at the two armpits.
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ | Vajrasūrya at the two eyes.
Oṃ phaṭ haṃ | Hayagrīva is in all the limbs. [This is] the weapon-mantra (astra).
Oṃ vaṃ | Vajravārāhī at the navel. Oṃ hāṃ yoṃ | Yāminī at the heart.
Oṃ hrīṃ moṃ | Mohinī at the forehead.
Oṃ hreṃ hrīṃ | Saṃcāriṇī on the head.
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ | Saṃtrāsinī on the crest-lock (śikhā).
Oṃ phaṭ phaṭ | On all the limbs of the Goddess.
Thus is the secondary means of accomplishment (upasādhana).
With the syllable *hūṃ* in the heart, one visualizes the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*) seated upon a moon disc.
*Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. The Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*) is at the throat.
Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasamvaraṃ svāhā. [One should visualize] the Body-Vajra on the forehead.
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | [This is] at the heart of the Goddess. Oṃ caurī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | [This is] at the throat.
Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā | [This is] at the forehead.
One should place the syllable Oṃ on the head, the syllable Hūṃ at the heart, the syllable Āḥ on the pericarp, the syllable Svā at the waist, and the syllable Hā on the pair of thighs.
Thus is the means of accomplishment.
Then, having become one arisen from the pledge of gnosis, the Vajra-holder is spoken of here;
having meditated upon the state of consecration, one should thereafter commence the worship.

Having joined the mantra in the two [syllables] at the *liṅga*, and having placed the syllable *a* on the human nose (*naranāsikā*), the wise one should join the syllable *vaṃ* likewise upon the *varaṭaka* of the *liṅga*; thus he should churn the Yoginī, becoming pure in body and free from disease.
This is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named Ādiyoga.

Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of passion of all the Tathāgatas. Having drawn in the Sugatas by means of the radiance from the seed-syllable in the heart, one should place them between the eyebrows at the station of Avadhūti.
Having meditated upon it as conjoined with the first vowel, it blazes up at that very moment.
Mounted upon a circle of firebrands, it likewise whirls among the ḍākinīs—
a wheel of an ocean of garlands of flames facing in every direction.

The four-faced Vīreśa, surrounded by heroic Ḍākinīs, has his channels pierced everywhere throughout the pathways of the subtle body according to the differentiation of the principles (tattvas). Having divided them at will, the practitioner of mantra should join those that were inverted.
One should prepare the great maṇḍala of supreme passion for the sake of practice.

In all the northern [directions], the ḍākinīs manifest the worlds. In the east is the white-blue-hued Ḍākinī; in the north, the pale-red-hued Lāmā; in the west, the red-pale-hued Khaṇḍarohā Ḍākinī; and in the south, the white-yellow-hued Rūpiṇī. All of these stand dancing upon corpses, holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup in their hands, with flaming hair rising upward, adorned with all ornaments, three-eyed, and one-faced. Within the skull-cups are, according to the rule, an elephant, a jackal, a human, and a snake.
In Vidiśā, however, there are four [temples], each with no fewer than five *karoṭaka* domes;
they are adorned with images of the Buddha and provided with crests.
In Pullīramalaya, on the head, are the Khaṇḍakapālin [deities]; Pracaṇḍā carries nails and teeth.
In Jālandhara, at the crest-lock, is Mahākaṅkāla-Caṇḍākṣī, who carries away hair and body hair;
in Oḍyāna, at the right ear, is Kaṅkālaprabhāvatī, who carries away the impurities of the skin;
and in Arbuda, at the spinal column, is Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin-Mahānāsā, who carries away flesh.
In the directions starting from the east, in reverse order.
In Godāvarī, at the left ear, Surāvairiṇī and Vīramatī always carry the *nāhu*.
In Rāmeśvara, between the eyebrows, Amitābhā and Kharvarī carry the garland of bones (*asthimālā*).
In Devīkoṭa, at the two eyes, Laṅkeśvarī carries Vajraprabhā.

In Mālava, at the base of the arms, is Vajradehadrumacchāyā, who brings about the birth from the heart-mandala; these are situated in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast. These are the Khecarīs of the Citta-cakra, established through meditative union (samāpatti). Likewise, in Kāmarūpa, at the armpits, is Aṅgulikā-Erāvatī, who constantly carries the eye.
In Oḍra, at the pair of breasts, is Vajrajaṭilā-Mahābhairavā, who brings bile;
in Triśakuni, at the navel, is Mahāvīrā-Vāyuvegā, who brings the lungs;
in Kosala, at the nose, is Vajrahūṃkāra-Surābhakṣī, who brings the garland of intestines.
In the directions starting from the east:
in Kaliṅga, at the mouth, is Subhadraśyāmādevī, known as Pārśvatantu;
in Lampāka, at the throat, is Vajrabhadrasubhadrā; and in the belly, she bears Gardabhī.
In the heart of Kāñcī is Mahābhairavī; Hayakarṇā is in Viṣṭhāva;
Virūpākṣī and Khagānanā are in Himālaya at the penis and situated in the middle of the hair-parting.
As before, they are in the intermediate directions. These Bhūcaryas of the Vākcakra are established through meditative absorption (samāpatti). || 36 ||
In the *liṅga* of Pretādhivāsinī, Mahābalacakravegā always carries phlegm (*śleṣman*).
In the anus of Gṛhadevatā, however, Ratnavajrakhaṇḍarohā constantly carries pus (*pūya*).
In the thighs of Saurāṣṭrā, Hayagrīvaśauṇḍinī is proclaimed to be the carrier of blood (*rakta*).
In the two shanks, on Suvarṇadvīpa, are Ākāśagarbha and Cakravarmiṇī, who bring forth perspiration. In the directions starting from the east,
in the city of Aṅgulī, are Mārāri and Suvīrā, who bring forth fat.
On the back of the foot, in the region of Sindhu, Padmanarteśvara and Mahābalā constantly carry tears.
On the big toe, in Maru, Vairocanacakravartinī and Kheṭāvahā [reside].
At the knee, in Kulatā, Vajrasattva and Mahāvīryā carry a young lion.
As before, in the intermediate directions, the Pātālavāsinyas of the Body-Cakra are established through meditative absorption.
At the eastern gate is Kākāsyā;
at the northern [gate] is Ulūkāsyā.
Śvānāsyā is in the west;
Śūkarāsyā is in the south.
Endowed with the colors and symbols of the ḍākinīs and others,
mounted upon corpses, blazing with light, and all possessing distorted faces,
the female messengers (dūtīs) are stationed in both direct and reverse order. (38)
In the southeast is Yamadāḍhī;
in the southwest is Yamadūtī;
and in the northwest is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī.
And Yamamathanī is indeed in the northeast.
Two by two, the colors are beautiful;
as before, they are mounted upon horses.
Śrī Heruka and the other heroes have their hands engaged in embracing the vajra and bell.
All the goddesses hold skull-bowls in their hands and are imbued with the sentiments of love (śṛṅgāra) and the rest.
Mounted upon corpses, blazing with light, they stand upon the sun and perform the tāṇḍava dance.
They possess three eyes, have fearsome fangs, and are adorned with garlands of skulls.
Bearing garlands of many rays, their eyes and glances are crooked like the waves of a frown;
those known as Kākāsyā and the others are described as wearing garments of tiger skins.
They wear necklaces, crest-jewels, armlets, diamond threads, and earrings.
With garlands of heads adorning their necks and ankle-bells at their feet,
they stand in the pratyālīḍha posture;
these twenty-four upward-facing heroes are born from the limbs of Śrī Heruka.
The twenty-four ḍākinīs are born from the womb of Vārāhī.
Therefore, the Vajrī is said here to be born from the *jñānasamaya*.
Having meditated upon the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should thereafter commence the worship.
Thus, everything should be performed as before.
Now, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are to be established through the yoga of the deities.
The application of mindfulness to the body is Ḍākinī; the application of mindfulness to feelings is Lāmā;
the application of mindfulness to phenomena is Khaṇḍarohā.
The application of mindfulness to the mind is Rūpiṇī;
the production of the supernormal power of desire is Pracaṇḍā;
and the production of the supernormal power of vigor is Caṇḍākṣī.
Prabhāvatī is the manifestation of the supernatural power of investigation;
Mahānāsā is the manifestation of the supernatural power of the mind;
Vīramatī is the faculty of faith.
The faculty of energy is Kharvarī; the faculty of mindfulness is Laṅkeśvarī;
the faculty of concentration is Drumacchāyā.
The faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī;
the power of faith is Mahābhairavā;
the power of vigor is Vāyuvegā.
The power of mindfulness is Surābhakṣī;
the power of concentration is Śyāmādevī;
the power of wisdom is Subhadrā.
Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration; Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is vigor;
Cakravegā is the factor of awakening that is joy.
The factor of enlightenment of tranquility is Khaṇḍarohā;
the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena is Śauṇḍinī;
the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is Cakravarmiṇī.
Suvīrā is the factor of awakening that is equanimity;
Mahābalā is right view;
Cakravartinī is right intention.
Right speech is Mahāvīryā; right action is Kākāsyā; right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā.
Right effort is Śvānāsyā;
right mindfulness is Śūkarāsyā;
[right concentration is the Blessed One, Śrī Heruka].
The generation of unarisen wholesome states is Yamadāḍhī; the preservation of arisen wholesome states is Yamadūtī;
and the abandonment of arisen unwholesome states is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī.
The non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states is the "Yamamathanī" [mudrā].

"Yamadāḍhī is the producer [of the unwholesome states]... [she is] for the abandonment of unwholesome states that have arisen," so said the Blessed One, the Vajrī, regarding the purification of the deities of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma).
[One should visualize] a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp situated in the center of one's own heart.
In its center stands the channel (nāḍī), having the nature of oil and fire;
it hangs downward like a plantain flower.
In its center resides the Hero (vīra), the size of a mustard seed.
The syllable *Hūṃ* is the unstruck seed-syllable (*anāhata-bīja*), flowing like snow;
it is renowned as "Spring" (*vasanta*), the delighter in the hearts of embodied beings.
Vārāhī, in the form of the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*), is considered to be the *tilaka*.
Shaken by the winds of karma and blazing in the circle of the navel, she becomes satisfied upon reaching the Spring (Vasanta) and remains established through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
This is the hero Śrī Heruka; he is considered the *Vasantatilakā*.
Having assumed the form of emptiness, he abides within the moving and the unmoving;
through the divisions of body, speech, and mind, he issues forth by way of the three gates.
Abiding within all bodies, he effects coming and going.
The short vowel is proclaimed as the form of the syllable *na*,

while in the heart, the syllable *hūṃ* is remembered as having two long measures (*mātrā*). At the throat, it is said to be in the form of the syllable *oṃ*, with three measures, known as the protracted (*pluta*).
On the forehead is that syllable *haṃ*, the resonance (*nāda*), the point (*bindu*), and the unstruck sound (*anāhata*).
Through the differentiation of the four wheels, there are the great elements beginning with earth.
Abiding in the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), it arises from the four lotuses. (Padma = moment?)
Devoted to the four yogas through the form of the four joys,
and through the relationship of action and agent in the form of supreme bliss,
he sports here at ease in the form of Śrī Vajrasattva.
Established in the four groups of petals in the four cardinal directions are the four elemental channels (bhūtanāḍī), which take on the nature of oil and fire. Furthermore,
there are four channels situated in the intermediate directions that also extend into them.
Flowing with the five nectars, they have attained the nature of that worship;
they are renowned as the "fourfold worship," for in reality they are of that very form.
Thus, eight channels are established within the center of the heart of the body.
60 & 61 (ex conj.): Twenty-four others are proclaimed according to the divisions of body, speech, and mind;
they reside in various locations, relying upon the distinctions of the *pīṭhas* and so forth.
"Kākāsyā and the others are, as before, the purifiers of Pātāla and so forth.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord Vajrī, the cause of sealing.
Having first visualized the ten substances within a skull-cup born from the syllable *A*, [one should proceed].
One should perform the blazing and heating of the mandala of wind and fire;
having meditated upon it joined with the first syllable, it blazes up at that very moment.
One should contemplate the tantra-mantra as being joined with the reversed syllables.
Everything is illuminated by the syllable Oṃ; thus the three principles (tritattva) have been proclaimed.
One should meditate in this way, O Goddess, for it bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of substances.
Through this, the perfection of yoga occurs and realization arises. (66)
Sugiki notes that the Tibetan version continues with a "mantra collection."
